name: Uncanny Valley
description: As an artificial character's human likeness increases, emotional response grows more positive -- until, just short of true human likeness, it plunges sharply into revulsion and unease, before recovering again once likeness becomes genuinely indistinguishable from a real human.
design_relevance_note: The standard caution against near-photorealistic avatars, virtual assistants, and CGI/robotic character design -- informs deliberate stylization choices in avatar and voice-assistant design specifically to stay clear of the dip.
myth_risk_note: The core effect is robust at meta-analytic scale, but popular design discourse often overstates it as a single clean dip rather than the finding's own more nuanced result -- effect size varies meaningfully by how human-likeness was manipulated (face-distortion vs. naturalistic morphing techniques), a real nuance worth flagging even though the underlying effect itself isn't a myth.
prevalence_note: Near-universal reference point in any discussion of realistic character or avatar design, well beyond academic robotics.

findings.description: As a robot or artificial character's human likeness increases, people's emotional response grows more positive — up to a point. Just before reaching true, indistinguishable human likeness, the response abruptly plunges from empathy to revulsion and unease, a steep dip termed the 'uncanny valley,' before recovering again as likeness becomes genuinely indistinguishable from a real human. Proposed as a hypothesis in a relatively obscure 1970 essay, largely unnoticed for decades before becoming widely influential in robotics, animation, and AI-avatar design discourse.

The first meta-analysis of the uncanny valley effect, synthesizing 247 effect sizes from 72 studies (of 468 screened), found a large overall effect (Hedges' g = 1.01), confirming Mori's core hypothesis holds up robustly at scale despite decades of individual studies producing mixed and inconsistent results. Effect size varied meaningfully by how human-likeness was manipulated in the study — face-distortion techniques produced the largest effect, more naturalistic morphing techniques produced smaller ones — a real methodological reason earlier individual studies looked inconsistent with each other.
findings.effect_size: overall Hedges' g = 1.01, 95% CI [0.80, 1.22]; ranging from g=0.94 (morphing) to g=1.46 (face distortion) depending on stimulus-creation technique
findings.source_title: A Meta-analysis of the Uncanny Valley's Independent and Dependent Variables

applications.title: The Polar Express (2004): motion-capture realism widely panned as 'dead-eyed' despite box-office success
applications.description: Warner Bros.' The Polar Express (2004), directed by Robert Zemeckis, was among the first feature films built entirely on motion-capture animation aimed at photorealistic human characters. Multiple named film critics singled out the characters' near-human-but-not-quite appearance as unsettling rather than immersive: Peter Travers (Rolling Stone) called the result 'a failed and lifeless experiment in which everything goes wrong', Stephanie Zacharek (Salon) said the look gave her 'the creeps', Geoff Pevere (Toronto Star) said it would cause 'nightmares', and Paul Clinton (CNN) described it as 'disconcerting, and at worst, a wee bit horrifying'. Rotten Tomatoes' own critical consensus states plainly that 'the animation for the human characters isn't lifelike enough'. The film was nonetheless a commercial success (a worldwide gross of $318.2 million against a $165-170 million budget, and a rare A+ CinemaScore from audiences), illustrating that the uncanny-valley reaction can coexist with -- and not fully override -- a film's commercial and audience reception.
applications.industry_context: Feature-film animation / motion-capture technology, not a digital product interface -- included as one of the field's most widely-cited real examples of the uncanny valley outside HCI/robotics specifically.
applications.ethical_note: This is a technology-execution shortfall, not an attempt to persuade or manipulate an audience -- Zemeckis and Warner Bros. were pursuing realism, not exploiting a psychological blind spot for gain. No persuasion or manipulation dimension exists here to grade; the negative reaction is a pure perceptual/craft issue, the same distinction this graph's ethical_risk field draws between intent-bearing and intent-free cases.
